messages.subject: regressing out batch effects
messages.body_plain:
I need to deal with some batch effects in our data and am not quite sure what the optimal way to do so would be....  Our experimental design is that we have one treated and one untreated tissue section in each batch, so treatment effects are not confounded by batch effects.  It is clear though in the PCA plots that there are some strong batch effects present and I am thinking that it would be ideal to normalize or batch effect correct prior to performing segmentation analyses.

One way that I am thinking I could deal with this is that I could model the relationship between ion intensity and batches and then take the residuals as the scaled data and move forward with the remainder of the analyses.

Has anyone done this before? I imagine that I should attempt to remove batch effects after pre-processing is done.

Thanks,
Nadia

messages.subject: Re: regressing out batch effects
messages.body_plain:
Hi Nadia,

Could you clarify why you need to do normalization prior to segmentation? Normally segmentation is performed separately for each tissue section, and is not affected by tissue batches.

What you suggest is a constant normalization, where you multiply (or subtract of the log scale) a constant to equalize medians or some other summary of the intensities in each run. Besides not affecting the segmentation, it will assume that all the locations in the tissue and all the ions are effected by the batch in a same way. This is a quite strong assumption.

Another option can be to find segments first, map the segments between the tissues, and compare those. These will indeed require between-batch normalization, but at least in can be more region-specific.

HTH
Olga

Thank you for your reply.  This is a really good point.... we cannot be sure that all locations in the tissue and all ions are affected by batch in the same way... and I actually doubt that they are. Lastly, I am very interested in mapping the identified segments between tissues.  I have looked through the Cardinal documentation and don't see a mention of that (or I am missing it).  Would you mind pointing me in the right direction as to where I can find information on how to do this?

Thank you so much for your time,
Nadia

messages.subject: Re: regressing out batch effects
messages.body_plain:
Hi Nadia,

You are correct, with two caveats. (1) We do not have an automated procedure for mapping segments between tissues. In the past we have done this manually, using the understanding of the experimental context/known markers/available annotations etc. This may be non-trivial. (2) If you pre-process each batch separately, your list of m/z may be different between the batches. (The problem would go away if you could process all the tissues together. But the file size may be too large for that). So you may need to match the m/z between the batches. You can also try to do this manually. Or, I am wondering if Kylie has any words of wisdom regarding that ;-)

Sorry for not having an easy solution ;-)

Sincerely
Olga

Thank you Olga,

I will move forward with the statistical test then.  However, the mapping across tissue sections is definitely a challenge....

So what I have been doing to process the various samples is that I read the imzml file from each sample in separately, I then apply mass binning through mzBin() and process() so that the number of rows are the same for each sample (and so that they have the same resolution).  I then use cbind() to bind all the samples together so that the rest of the pre-processing is done on all samples together.  So my understanding is that the m/z match then (unless I am mistaken).  The file size is quite large, but I am working on a high-memory HPC system so it was okay.

I am definitely eager to hear whether Kylie has any words of wisdom on this.  I"m trying to get a handle on this now before our dataset becomes MUCH larger :)

Thanks,
Nadia

messages.body_plain:
Hi Nadia,

If the data is from a "continuous" format imzML and the m/z axes don't already match, then that is the best way to do it currently.

If the data is from a "processed" format imzML, then you can manually specify the mass range and resolution in readImzML() so that they match on import.

Making it easier to merge datasets in all cases is on my todo list for next version.

-Kylie
